title: Encrypted documents — how sealing works
html:
Encrypted documents — how sealing works

A document can ask the build to seal it: the artifact carries the body as authenticated ciphertext, and the reader locks the article behind a password. This page describes how to mark a document, how the password travels from a build to a reader, and what stays public; the algorithm, the build-side mechanics and the boundaries of the scheme follow for reference. The product summary lives in README.md, the architecture in docs/design.md.

Marking a document

A document's front matter can ask the build to seal it. The key is encrypt:

Front matterMeaning
(no key), encrypt: false, encrypt:Build the document as usual
encrypt: trueSeal it with the global password
encrypt: "secret"Seal it with this document's own password
anything else (encrypt: "", a number, a list, invalid YAML)Fail the build with an error naming the document
---
title: Private notes
encrypt: true
---

Nobody reads this without the password.

A document with a password of its own unlocks independently of every other sealed document; encrypt: true documents share one password, so the reader never asks for the same one twice in a session.

Providing the password

The global password takes the same three sources as every setting, in the same order — --password over WIKICC_PASSWORD over the configuration file's password key.

WIKICC_PASSWORD="opensesame" wikicc path/to/docs
wikicc path/to/docs --password "opensesame" # works, but the password lands in the shell history

A document that asks for encryption and finds no password anywhere fails the build: exit code 1, the error names the document on stderr, and nothing is written, whatever --strict says. There is no plaintext fallback — a build never ships a sealed declaration unsealed.

Two details about the sources:

  • A command line --password stays in the shell history and the process list, so prefer WIKICC_PASSWORD.
  • The variable's value is trimmed, which makes the configuration file the only source that can carry a password with leading or trailing whitespace (its values are read verbatim).

What stays public

The title stays public. The lock page, the sidebar, the link graph and search all show the title; search reaches the body only after the reader unlocks the document — before that, a query matching the title finds a row marked Locked, and afterwards the document is ordinary (search describes the two halves). What the lock page shows is exactly what the artifact leaks: the id and the title, the same metadata the reader uses everywhere.

The reader

The reader shows a locked document on a lock page that carries the password field itself — the reader types where they stand, and a correct password renders the article in place. The form answers only after the reader has silently tried the passwords the session already holds, so documents sealed with one password never ask twice within a session. A reference to a sealed chapter offers the same field inside its hover preview, so the unlock happens where the reading happens.

Unlocked passwords live in the session's memory alone — nothing is written to localStorage, sessionStorage or a cookie — so reloading the page relocks every document, and a fresh session asks again.

Threat model

The scheme protects artifacts at rest: a copied single-html file, a published pages folder, an html-dir archive — opened in a text editor they show no body, no chapter structure and no password. It does not protect the source folder — the Markdown files and the password a build was handed live in the clear on the machine that builds — and it does not protect anything against a reader who holds the password.

The password is the security. The salt, the nonce and the iteration count are public parameters that weaken nothing; a short password does.

Algorithm and parameters

  • AES-256-GCM seals the body. The cipher is authenticated, so a wrong password, a wrong document binding and a tampered byte are one and the same failure, and the ciphertext layout is ciphertext || 16-byte tag — what both the RustCrypto crate and the Web Crypto API emit.
  • PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 derives the 256-bit key from the password and the salt, at 600,000 iterations (the OWASP recommendation).
  • Per-document parameters. Every sealed document gets a fresh random 16-byte salt and 12-byte nonce at build time, so the derivation input never repeats across documents or builds.
  • AAD binding. The document id travels as the AES-GCM additionalData, so a ciphertext cannot be transplanted into another document's blob.
  • Plaintext shape. The sealed plaintext is the whole document model — canonical JSON {html, toc, blocks, text} — so a sealed article leaks neither body nor chapter structure; the title stays public metadata.
  • Format version. The sealed blob leads with its own v, the crypto format's version, checked where the blob is opened.

The two ends interoperate over one parameter set, pinned by fixed interop vectors committed to both test suites (src/crypto.rs and tests/js/lock.test.js): either side drifting fails both at once. file:// pages are a trustworthy context in Chrome, Edge and Firefox, so crypto.subtle is available and the scheme needs no JavaScript fallback.

The build side

encrypt.rs reads the encrypt field out of the raw front-matter text the markdown AST carries — extracted during the one markdown parse, no second pass — against the strict matrix above. The global password comes from the three sources in their precedence.

The sealing pass runs on the assembled bundle, after the favicon registration and before the diagnostics are reported. It empties the four content fields of a sealed DocModel, writes the blob into its enc field, and leaves edges and every public metadata alone. The payload shapes stay optional: DocModel.enc, ManifestDoc.enc and ChunkPayload.enc are skipped when unset, so a site without encryption serialises byte-identically to a build that never heard of the feature, and the search.json entry of a sealed document carries {id, title} alone, so no body text reaches the browser before an unlock.

The asset boundary

A sealed document is self-contained. Before the body is encrypted, its own asset placeholders — in the body and in every chapter block — are expanded into data: URIs built from the asset table's MIME type and bytes, the construction the single-html writer inlines with, so the sealed body is self-contained and renders its images natively once unlocked. After all documents are sealed, the asset table is pruned to what the public documents and the favicon still address, and stats.assets and stats.asset_bytes are decremented to match:

  • an asset referenced only by sealed documents travels inside the ciphertext and is not written to the artifact at all;
  • an asset shared with a public document is written once, for the public reference, and the decrypted body carries its own embedded copy besides.
